```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(bwebs)
```

This vignette goes through the whole workflow on the invented example
community of the package and explains the methodological decisions behind
each step: how links are inferred, how their probabilities are calibrated,
how the default matching rule was chosen and how it performs on an
independent food web.

## 1. The community and its nodes

A community is described by two tables. The **nodes** have one row per taxon
(or non-taxonomic resource, such as detritus), with its classification
aligned with the names of the registry, its role and its rank of
identification:

```{r}
example_taxa[, c("node_id", "taxon", "rank", "role", "family", "order", "class")]
```

The **community** has one row per sample and node, in long format, with an
abundance or biomass. Only presence is used: a node is present when its value
is greater than `threshold` (0 by default). A zero is an observed absence;
`NA` is unknown and is never treated as an absence.

```{r}
head(example_community)
```

`prepare_nodes()` validates the nodes and computes, for each node and role,
the levels at which it is matched with the registry. Detritus is matched by
name and alias; producers and detritus never consume; the shrimp
*Dugastella valentina*, absent from the registry, takes the records of
*Asellus* through an explicit surrogate.

```{r}
nodes <- prepare_nodes(example_taxa)
nodes
```

## 2. The metaweb and the evidence of each link

`build_metaweb()` infers the potential links with the WebBuilder logic of
Gray et al. (2015): a link resource → consumer exists if a record of the
registry matches both nodes at their levels. The default `matching_rule()`
starts at family level and climbs to order and class until a node links with
at least five other nodes of the community, using every registry at every
level (section 4 shows how this rule was chosen).

```{r}
mw <- build_metaweb(nodes, gray2015)
mw
head(mw$edges[, c("resource", "consumer", "support", "n_sources", "evidence_class")])
```

Each link keeps the **class of evidence** of its best supporting record: the
taxonomic generalisation needed to reach it (`exact` when the record names
the node itself, then `genus`, `subfamily`, `family`, `order`, `class`, or
`generic` for generic resources such as "Algae").

## 3. Calibration: how often are inferred links observed?

A metaweb built from a compilation contains links that are not realised in a
given community, and more so the more taxonomic generalisation they needed.
`validate_rule()` measures this on the registry itself: each validation
study (a whole community with recorded diets) is left out in turn, rebuilt
from the rest of the registry with the same rule, and the inferred links are
compared with those recorded in it.

Studies of the same system share records. If one of them stays in the
registry while the other is rebuilt, its records predict the other and the
probabilities are overestimated. `shared_studies()` finds them:

```{r}
validation_webs <- gray2015_sources$study_id[gray2015_sources$validation]
shared_studies(gray2015, validation_webs, threshold = 0.2)
```

62% of the links of study 13 are also recorded in study 50, so the two are
left out together (`groups`). Study 12 is Tuesday Lake (section 5).

`calibrate_links()` then fits a logistic model with one coefficient per
class of evidence and a random effect of the web to the counts of inferred
and observed links. It is a Bayesian model: the coefficients have normal
priors (standard deviation `prior_sd = 1.5` on the logit scale) and the
standard deviation of the web effect a half-normal prior (scale
`prior_sigma = 2.5`); the web effects are integrated out by adaptive
Gauss-Hermite quadrature and the posterior is sampled by Metropolis-Hastings
(`diagnostics$rhat` should be close to 1 and `diagnostics$ess` large). The
package includes the calibration of the Gray et al. (2015) registry with the
default rule:

```{r}
gray2015_calibration
gray2015_calibration$webs[, c("study_id", "n_consumers", "n_predicted", "precision")]
```

`p_average` is the probability in a web with an average effect and `p_new`
the probability in a new system, averaged over web effects. Two results
matter for the interpretation:

* Links supported by records of the same genus are observed more often than
  links that needed a family or an order: the class of evidence is
  informative. The probability does not fall steadily with the
  generalisation, though: links of the same taxon are observed less often
  than links of the same genus, and links that needed a class about as
  often.
* The proportion of inferred links that are observed varies a lot between
  webs (the standard deviation of the web effect on the logit scale is
  `r round(gray2015_calibration$sigma, 2)`): part of it reflects differences
  between systems, part how completely each web was described.

The probability of a link is the probability of observing it in a comparable,
well-studied community. Because validation webs miss rare links, it is a
lower bound for the existence of the link. Pairs without an inferred link are
not modelled: in a registry web a taxon is listed because it eats or is
eaten, so the rate of links among pairs that were not inferred in those webs
does not transfer to communities sampled independently of their diets.

Which studies count as whole communities is a scientific decision. The
bundled calibration uses a provisional set (`gray2015_sources$validation`);
to use another one, validate and calibrate again (a few minutes):

```{r, eval = FALSE}
my_sources <- c("27", "13", "50", "12", "59", "63", "11", "15", "58", "46", "49")
v <- validate_rule(gray2015, sources = my_sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")))
my_calibration <- calibrate_links(v, seed = 1)
```

## 4. Choosing the matching rule and the sources

How far should a node climb, and from where? `score_rule()` answers with a
cross-validated **Brier score**: each validation system is left out of the
calibration in turn, its inferred links take the probability of their class
in a new system under the calibration fitted to the other systems, pairs
without an inferred link take probability 0, and the squared errors against
the recorded links are averaged over all the pairs of the web (lower is
better). A missed link costs 1, an inferred link of probability \(p\) costs
\((1 - p)^2\) when it is real and \(p^2\) when it is not, so the score
rewards both finding the links and giving them the right probabilities. The
`skill` compares it with a null model that gives every pair the mean
connectance of the other systems, and `tss` is the true skill statistic of
the deterministic metaweb, as in Gray et al. (2015).

`compare_rules()` scores a list of rules on the same webs; `candidate_rules()`
is the grid of 21 rules (fixed matching at the taxon, genus, family or
order; climbing from genus or family to order or class with thresholds of 1
or 5 partners; the WebBuilder ladder up to family, order or class; three
rules without downward inheritance). With the Gray registry alone (Tuesday
Lake kept apart, section 5), the comparison takes about half an hour, so its
result is included:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
registry <- gray2015[gray2015$study_id != "12", ]   # Tuesday Lake kept apart
sources <- setdiff(validation_webs, "12")
cmp <- compare_rules(registry, sources = sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")), seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
gray2015_rule_comparison[, c("rule", "brier", "brier_diff", "brier_diff_se", "skill", "tss",
                             "precision", "recall")]
```

Climbing from family to class had the lowest score. The threshold (one or
five partners) and the downward inheritance made no difference larger than
its standard error; starting at genus, using the ladder of Gray et al.
(2015) or matching at a fixed level scored worse, and matching only the
taxon itself scored worst. With the Gray registry alone the skill of every
rule is slightly negative: a third of the recorded links are not inferred.

The eight main rules were then scored with records of Global Biotic
Interactions (GloBI, section 9) for the consumers of the validation webs,
alone and combined with the Gray registry. When each web was rebuilt, the
GloBI studies holding at least 10% of its links (copies of that web in
other compilations) were left out too (`validate_rule(exclusions = )`):

```{r}
source_comparison[1:12, c("source", "primary_registry", "supplementary_max_level", "rule",
                          "brier", "diff_vs_gray", "diff_vs_gray_se", "skill", "recall")]
```

Both registries used at every level (no primary registry) with the default
rule scored best, and this combination sets the defaults of
`matching_rule()`. GloBI raised the share of recorded links that are inferred
from two thirds to nine tenths without lowering the precision (about 40%),
and the skill became positive. Using GloBI only up to family
(`primary_registry = "gray2015"`, `supplementary_max_level = "family"`)
scored worse than using it at every level. GloBI holds secondary
compilations (metawebs and trait databases) that may contain the
validation webs generalised to family or order, which the exclusions by
shared links do not detect; without them the scores were nearly the same
(`dev/validation/source_sensitivity.R` in the GitHub repository of the
package). The rule itself was again best climbing from family, with any
source.

## 5. An independent test: Tuesday Lake

The Tuesday Lake food webs of 1984 and 1986 (Cohen et al. 2003; Jonsson et
al. 2005), from the cheddar package (Hudson et al. 2013), are an independent
test: study 12 of the registry is Tuesday Lake, so it was left out of the
registry and of the validation webs while the rules and the sources were
compared, and so were the GloBI studies that copy it.

```{r}
head(tuesday_lake_taxa[, c("node_id", "taxon", "rank", "role", "family", "class")])
table(tuesday_lake_links$sample_id)
```

`score_metaweb()` compares a metaweb with an observed web. For the test, the
metaweb is built from the registry without study 12 and the calibration is
fitted to the other 12 webs:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
v <- validate_rule(registry, sources = sources, groups = list(c("13", "50")))
cal <- calibrate_links(v, seed = 2026)
mw_tl <- build_metaweb(prepare_nodes(tuesday_lake_taxa), registry)
tl84 <- tuesday_lake_links[tuesday_lake_links$sample_id == "TL84", ]
present <- tuesday_lake_community$node_id[tuesday_lake_community$sample_id == "TL84"]
score_metaweb(mw_tl, cal, tl84, nodes = present)
```

The scores on Tuesday Lake (mean of the two years) are in the same tables:

```{r}
source_comparison[1:12, c("source", "rule", "tl_brier", "tl_skill", "tl_tss", "tl_precision",
                          "tl_recall")]
```

The default inferred about 70% of the observed links (a fifth with the Gray
registry alone, mostly British streams with few diets of plankton) and had
a positive skill; the ranking of the combinations on Tuesday Lake agreed
with the cross-validation (Spearman correlation 0.73). Two weaknesses
remain. Links inferred from generic resources ("Algae" extended to every
alga) are frequent in the validation streams but rare in this plankton web,
so their calibrated probability is too high there. And the webs sampled
from the metaweb have too many basal species and too low a mean trophic
level: sampling can only remove links of the metaweb, not add those it
misses.

## 6. Plausible metawebs

`sample_metawebs()` takes the coefficients and the standard deviation of the
web effect of each draw from the posterior draws of the calibration and,
with `system = "random"`, draws the effect of the system, and keeps each link
with the probability of its class. One realisation of the metaweb is shared
by all the samples of the community in each draw.

```{r}
draws <- sample_metawebs(mw, gray2015_calibration, n_draws = 100, seed = 2026)
draws
head(draws$links[, c("resource", "consumer", "evidence_class", "p_mean", "inclusion")])
```

With `system = "average"` the system effect is fixed at 0 (a community like
the average validation web) and the intervals are narrower; a number fixes it
at that value on the logit scale.

## 7. Indicators of every sample

`calc_indicators()` builds the web of each sample in each draw (the nodes
present plus the permanent resources) and computes the indicators of
`web_indicators()` on the web without cannibalism and without isolated nodes,
aggregated into trophic species. Modularity (with igraph) and robustness are
optional because they are slower.

```{r}
ind <- calc_indicators(draws, example_community, permanent = c("cpom", "fpom"))
head(ind$values[, c("draw", "sample_id", "S", "L", "C", "TL_mean", "prop_omnivores")])
table(ind$values$status)
```

In draws with a very negative system effect the metaweb keeps few links, and
a sample can be left without any: its indicators are then undefined
(`status = "empty_web"`), not zero. By default the summaries report such
draws as missing; with `na_rm = TRUE` they are left out and counted in
`n_missing`, and the summaries then describe the draws where the indicator is
defined.

## 8. Summaries and contrasts

`summarize_indicators()` summarises the draws by sample or by groups of
samples; `contrast_indicators()` compares groups within each draw, which
keeps the uncertainty shared by all the samples of a draw out of the
contrast.

```{r}
summarize_indicators(ind, indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"), samples = example_samples,
                     by = "treatment", na_rm = TRUE)[, c(1:7, 13)]
contrast_indicators(ind, example_samples, by = "treatment", reference = "control",
                    indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"), na_rm = TRUE)[, c(1, 3:8, 10)]
```

The deterministic metaweb gives the reference values of the potential webs:

```{r}
det <- calc_indicators(mw, example_community, permanent = c("cpom", "fpom"))
summarize_indicators(det, indicators = c("S", "C", "TL_mean"),
                     samples = example_samples, by = "treatment")[, 1:4]
```

## 9. GloBI and other registries

`fetch_globi()` downloads trophic interactions from Global Biotic
Interactions and `globi_to_registry()` converts them (an internet connection
is needed, so this is not run here). Query each consumer of the community by
name, genus and family, as for `gray2015_globi_calibration`. GloBI already
contains the Gray et al. (2015) and Brose et al. (2005) compilations, which
are dropped by default, and other copies of classic food webs: check them
with `shared_studies()`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
taxa <- unique(c(example_taxa$taxon, example_taxa$genus, example_taxa$family))
raw <- fetch_globi(taxa[!is.na(taxa)], cache_dir = "globi_cache")
globi <- globi_to_registry(raw)
both <- combine_registries(gray2015, globi)
mw2 <- build_metaweb(nodes, both)
draws2 <- sample_metawebs(mw2, gray2015_globi_calibration, n_draws = 100, seed = 2026)
```

`gray2015_globi_calibration` is the calibration of the default rule with the
Gray registry combined with GloBI (13 validation webs, with the GloBI copies
of each web left out when it was rebuilt):

```{r}
gray2015_globi_calibration
```

A metaweb and its calibration must use the same rule and the same
registries: `sample_metawebs()` warns when the registries differ, because
the probability of each class of evidence depends on them, and links
supported only by registries outside the calibration have no probability
(`uncalibrated = `). To calibrate another combination, validate it with the
GloBI records of the consumers of the validation webs
(`validate_rule(train_registries = , exclusions = )`; see
`dev/globi/` and `dev/validation/` in the GitHub repository of the
package).
